text.p: Haile Gebrselassie ran alone through a warm, still Norwegian night on Friday to recapture the world 10,000 metres in one of the greatest exhibitions of distance running in track history.

The diminutive Ethiopian, who has not yet decided whether to bid for a hat-trick of world titles at the Athens world championships next month, took nearly seven seconds off Salah Hissou's year-old mark, clocking 26 minutes 31.32 seconds.

It was the 61st world record to fall at the Bislett Stadium, the fourth over 10,000, and nearly half a minute has now been sliced from the longest track event since Yobes Ondieki broke the 27-minute barrier here four years ago.
Less than a hour after Gebrselassie stepped off the track, Morocco's Hicham el Guerrouj made a bold bid on Noureddine Morceli's four-year-old world record in the Dream Mile.
El Guerrouj, who must now be poised to end Morceli's domination of the 1,500 and mile, was under world record pace at the bell but could not sustain his attack over the final 70 metres.
His time of 3:44.90 was still the second-fastest in history and only half a second outside Morceli's mark.
"I made a mistake at 950 metres when the pacemaker got too far ahead," said el Guerrouj. "I was disappointed after the race when I saw the board that I just missed the record."
The evening, though, belonged to Gebrselassie in his first appearance at the Bislett Games.
Four pacemakers, the final two of them from Ethiopia, did their job perfectly, pulling Gebrselassie through 4,000 metres nine seconds under world record schedule.
When Habte Jiftar dropped out with 14-1/2 laps still to run, Gebrselassie did not flag, clocking consistent 64 to 65-second lap times as he wove through the lapped runners.
With 1,000 metres left, Gebrselassie was still eight seconds under schedule and running with such confidence and determination that the world record and a $25,000 bonus was a formality.
"Bislett is a wonderful track for long distance running," he said. "If anyone breaks this I will take it back.
"I though I could have run even faster. Here the air is clean, the oxygen is good and the crowd is great.
"This season I will only run for records, I haven't made my mind up yet about running in the world championships. I will discuss it with my manager."
Earlier, Olympic and world champion Allen Johnson repelled a strong European challenge to set a year's best time in the 110 metres hurdles.
The American, unaffected by a total of four false starts before the race finally began, clocked 13.14, relegating Germany's Olympic bronze medallist Florian Schwarthoff to second place.
Schwarthoff clocked 13.21 with Britain's world silver medallist Tony Jarrett third in 13.30. Jarrett's compatriot Colin Jackson, the world record holder, was fourth 0.04 of a second further back.
Johnson, who said he would race three more times before the world championships, praised Schwarthoff's performance.
"We have had a lot of tough races over the years," he said. "It was a tough race, he is very strong."
Two Commonwealth athletes also set year's bests early in the meeting, first of the Golden Four series.
New Zealander Beatrice Faumuina threw a national record of 68.52 metres in the discus and Australia's Olympic silver medallist Cathy Freeman clocked 49.39 seconds in the women's 400 metres.

There was a fourth year's best for Romania's Gabriela Szabo, who clocked 14:42.43 in winning the women's 5,000, while American champion Marion Jones defeated Olympic champion Gail Devers in the women's 100 metres.
Devers, who has not qualified for the world championships, beat Jones over the same distance in Lausanne on Wednesday.
